title: Sort Matrix by Diagonals
statement:
`grid` is a square `n x n` matrix of integers. A diagonal here is the run of cells that begins at a cell of the first row or the first column and keeps stepping one row down and one column right until it leaves the matrix.

Rearrange the values inside each diagonal (a value never moves to another diagonal) and return the matrix, so that, reading every diagonal from its top-left end to its bottom-right end:

- each diagonal that begins in the first column, which includes the main diagonal from `grid[0][0]`, is in **non-increasing** order;
- each diagonal that begins in the first row to the right of `grid[0][0]` is in **non-decreasing** order.
notes:
## Intuition

Each diagonal starts at a cell of the first column (the main diagonal and everything below it) or of the first row (everything above it), and walking down-right from that cell visits exactly its cells. Diagonals never share cells, so each one can be fixed on its own: copy its values out, sort them in the order its triangle asks for, and pour them back along the same walk. A slower way that is easy to trust is to keep swapping any two neighbours on a diagonal that are out of order until no swap happens, like bubble sort.

## Approach

1. Write `sortDiagonal(row, col, descending)`: walk from `(row, col)` one step down and right at a time, collecting the cells into `values`; sort `values` largest-first when `descending` is true, smallest-first otherwise; walk again and write `values[k]` back into the `k`-th cell.
2. For every `row`, sort the diagonal that starts at `(row, 0)` in descending order. Row 0 gives the main diagonal.
3. For every `col` from 1, sort the diagonal that starts at `(0, col)` in ascending order.
4. Return `grid`, which was changed in place.

## Example 1, step by step

`grid = [[1,7,3],[9,8,2],[4,5,6]]`.

- `row = 0`: the main diagonal holds `[1, 8, 6]`; sorted descending it becomes `[8, 6, 1]`, written to `(0,0)`, `(1,1)`, `(2,2)`.
- `row = 1`: `[9, 5]` is already descending. `row = 2`: `[4]` is a single cell.
- `col = 1`: `[7, 2]` sorted ascending is `[2, 7]`, so `(0,1)` becomes 2 and `(1,2)` becomes 7.
- `col = 2`: `[3]` is a single cell.

The result is `[[8,2,3],[9,6,7],[4,5,1]]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n² log n): the diagonals cover all n² cells once, and each holds at most n values to sort.
- Space: O(n) for one diagonal's `values` at a time.

## Pitfalls

- The main diagonal belongs to the non-increasing group. Starting the ascending loop at `col = 0` would sort it a second time, the wrong way.
- Give `sort` a numeric comparator: the default compares text, so `[10, 9, -1]` would become `[-1, 10, 9]`.
- Both orders are read from the top-left end; write values back in the same direction you collected them.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | the size of the square grid |
| `sortDiagonal` | sorts the diagonal that starts at `(row, col)` |
| `row`, `col` | the first cell of a diagonal |
| `descending` | true for the main diagonal and those below it |
| `values` | that diagonal's values while they are sorted |
| `r`, `c` | the cell being visited on the diagonal |
| `k` | index of the sorted value written into `(r, c)` |
